summary: Extends POP3 to support international strings encoded in UTF-8 in user names, passwords, mail addresses, message headers and protocol text, so internationalized email can be fetched via POP3.

plainLanguage.summary: Lets a mailbox helper understand names and passwords written in any language's letters, not only plain English ones.

questions: how to use international email addresses with pop3
what is the pop3 utf8 command
how does pop3 handle non-ascii passwords
what does the pop3 lang command do
what is the pop3 utf8 response code
subtitle: How POP3 learns to carry UTF-8 text in mail, login names, passwords and server messages.

tldr.problem: POP3 was built for ASCII text. Internationalized email can put raw UTF-8 in headers and bodies, and users may have names and passwords outside ASCII, so the old protocol could not carry them.
tldr.mechanism: A new UTF8 capability and UTF8 command switch a session into UTF-8 mode, an optional USER argument allows UTF-8 credentials (prepared with SASLprep), and a LANG capability lets the client pick the language of server messages.
tldr.outcome: A server that cannot send a UTF-8 message to a client outside UTF-8 mode must send a surrogate message or refuse with an -ERR response. This RFC replaces the earlier experimental RFC 5721.

today: RFC 6856 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2013. It obsoletes RFC 5721, and the metadata shows no later RFC replacing or updating it.

sections.title: Why POP3 Needs UTF-8
sections.content:
RFC 6856 is part of the Email Address Internationalization protocols described in RFC 6530. Under that work, email can carry a Unicode string encoded in UTF-8 in the header, the body or both, and a maildrop read through POP3 might natively store Unicode characters.

The RFC extends POP3 using the POP3 extension mechanism of RFC 2449. It allows un-encoded UTF-8 in headers and bodies (for example sent with 8-bit content-transfer-encoding), adds support for login names and passwords containing UTF-8, allows UTF-8 in protocol-level response strings, and lets the client negotiate a language for those strings. It also adds one new response code, and it replaces the earlier experimental approach in RFC 5721.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail is moving to letters from every language. POP3, the mail pickup protocol, needs a way to say "I can handle those letters too".

sections.title: The UTF8 Capability and Command
sections.content:
The server advertises a UTF8 capability in its CAPA reply. The new UTF8 command, valid in the AUTHORIZATION state and with no parameters, switches the session from the ASCII-only mode of POP3 to UTF-8 mode. In that mode both sides can send and accept UTF-8 strings.

UTF-8 mode has no effect on messages in an ASCII-only maildrop. If a native maildrop is stored in UTF-8 or ASCII, messages go to the client as they are. If it uses some other encoding, the server SHOULD convert messages to UTF-8 first. MIME binary content-transfer-encoding is still not permitted, but 8bit is allowed.

Outside UTF-8 mode, the server MUST NOT send non-ASCII character strings as they are. If a client asks for a message that needs UTF-8 without having enabled the mode, the server MUST either send a surrogate message that complies with unextended POP and Internet Mail Format, or fail the request with an -ERR response. The size in a LIST reply SHOULD match the octets later sent in RETR. Clients MUST NOT issue STLS after UTF8.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a switch called UTF8. Until you flip it, the server only speaks plain letters and will not hand you a message it cannot write that way.

sections.title: UTF-8 Usernames and Passwords
sections.content:
If the server adds the USER argument to its UTF8 capability, it accepts UTF-8 usernames and passwords. The client MAY then use UTF-8 in USER, PASS or APOP, even before issuing the UTF8 command. If the argument is missing, clients MUST NOT use UTF-8 characters when authenticating.

Servers that offer it SHOULD apply SASLprep (RFC 4013) or a Standards Track successor to the USER and PASS arguments. A client or server that supports APOP and permits UTF-8 in names or passwords MUST apply SASLprep to the values used for the APOP digest. The server MUST reject UTF-8 that breaks the syntax of RFC 3629, and use of UTF-8 with the AUTH command follows the POP3 SASL mechanism.

The RFC explains that this part is optional because the implementation burden of SASLprep is not well understood, and requiring it everywhere could hurt deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can say "you may type your name and password in any alphabet". Both sides first tidy the text the same way, so the same word always looks identical when it is checked.

sections.title: Choosing a Language with LANG
sections.content:
POP3 lets most +OK and -ERR replies carry human-readable text, but RFC 1939 limits it to ASCII. The LANG capability adds a LANG command, valid in the AUTHORIZATION and TRANSACTION states, that asks the server to localize that text to a language matching the given language range.

On success the server answers +OK, a space, the exact language tag it chose, and another space, followed by text in that language, encoded in UTF-8. On failure it sends -ERR and keeps the previous language. The special argument asterisk asks for the language the server administrator prefers, which MAY vary with the active user. With no argument, the server lists each supported language as a language tag, optionally followed by a description of the language in that language.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the server which language to chat in. If it does not know that one, it keeps using the old one.

sections.title: Non-ASCII Maildrops and the UTF8 Response Code
sections.content:
When a server uses a native non-ASCII maildrop and is not in UTF-8 mode, it must still follow RFC 1939 and RFC 5322. If a message needs UTF-8 mode, the server MAY reject the download or MAY create and deliver a surrogate of the original message.

For rejections the RFC adds a UTF8 response code, valid on -ERR replies to LIST, TOP and RETR. It means the failure is due to a request for content containing UTF-8 while the client is not in UTF-8 mode. The client MAY try again after entering UTF-8 mode. The RFC admits that rejecting is unsatisfying, because the user may reach the message by some means and not others, and says upgrading both clients and servers is the only fully satisfactory fix.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for a letter the server can only show in the special alphabet, it says so, and you can flip the switch and ask again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of UTF-8 (RFC 3629), SASLprep (RFC 4013) and Unicode Format for Network Interchange (RFC 5198) apply, especially for UTF-8 usernames and passwords.

Two risks come from LANG. LANG * might reveal that a user exists, and their preferred language, to an active attacker if the language changes in response to USER, PASS or APOP before credentials are validated, so servers are strongly advised to offer a configuration that prevents this. A man-in-the-middle could also insert a LANG command and make diagnostic text unintelligible, which a session integrity mechanism such as STLS before LANG can defeat.

Changes to server authentication code for non-ASCII strings must be done with care to avoid vulnerabilities in parsing or matching.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting people pick a language can accidentally tell a snooper who has an account, and a meddler can scramble the language. Locking the connection first and being careful with the code prevents this.

data.title: Listing and choosing a language
data.code:
C: LANG
S: +OK Language listing follows:
S: en English
S: de Deutsch
S: it Italiano
S: .
C: LANG es
S: +OK es Idioma cambiado
C: LANG uga
S: -ERR es Idioma <<UGA>> no es conocido
